_readme: OPS-09. The engine is pinned to one llama.cpp commit on purpose — moving it
is its own decision with its own acceptance (CLAUDE.md hard constraint 1).
The cost of that rule is that 'we have not moved' and 'nobody has looked' are
indistinguishable from the outside, and an unreviewed pin ages into a known-
CVE pin without anyone deciding anything.
So the pin does not expire, but the REVIEW does. scripts/release_identity_gate.sh
fails once lastReviewed is older than reviewWindowDays, and the only way to
clear it is to look at the advisories and write down what was found. That
turns silence into a red gate instead of a comfortable default.
This file is not a vulnerability database. It records that a human compared
the pinned versions against upstream advisories on a date, and what they

components.name: llama.cpp
findings: Baseline entry created with this workstream (2026-08-30). No advisory was
triaged as part of creating the file; what it establishes is the review
obligation and its deadline, not a clean bill of health.
Reachability note for whoever does the first real review: the engine parses
attacker-influenced input on two surfaces — GGUF headers (curated models
only, SHA-256 pinned, so the exposure is a compromised curated file) and
the ggml-RPC wire between cluster nodes (peer-authenticated by PSK-TLS, so
the exposure is an already-admitted node). Advisories touching those two
are the ones that justify an out-of-band pin move.

components.name: client rust dependencies
findings: 2026-08-30, cargo-audit 0.21 against the RustSec database: ZERO vulnerability
advisories. 18 informational warnings, all of one shape — the gtk-rs GTK3
binding crates (atk, gdk*, gtk*, RUSTSEC-2024-0411..0420) are unmaintained,
plus proc-macro-error, unic-char-* and a yanked chacha20 0.10.1.
Assessment: the GTK3 crates arrive transitively through Tauri's Linux
webview stack and are not ours to move; 'unmaintained' is a supply-chain
signal (no upstream to fix a future bug), not a present vulnerability. The
yanked chacha20 is the one to watch — a yank usually has a reason, and it is
a crypto crate. Action for the next review: find out why 0.10.1 was yanked
and which dependency pulls it.

components.name: client javascript dependencies
findings: Checked mechanically by scripts/dependency_audit.sh via `pnpm audit`.
Baseline entry.

emergencyUpgradeChannel: An advisory that is reachable through one of the two surfaces above is the
one case where the pin moves without waiting for the normal acceptance cycle.
The sequence, so it is not improvised during an incident:
1. Move the pin in scripts/llamacpp-patches/UPSTREAM and reapply the patch
series; a patch that no longer applies is a stop, not a merge conflict to
2. Run scripts/ppl_gate.sh — the numerical acceptance is distribution-level,
so a rushed engine swap is still measured, just not re-baselined.
3. Ship it as a normal signed release plus a transparency-log entry.
4. Because the cluster's one invariant is that every node runs the same
engine version (hard constraint 4), an emergency bump SPLITS existing
clusters until every node updates. Say so in the release notes; a user
whose cluster stops forming after a security update and is not told why
will downgrade, which is the opposite of the intent.
5. Record the review here with the advisory id.
